This phenomenon is thought to occur because heightened emotional states increase our focus and awareness, leading to a greater number of memories being formed. As a result, when we later reflect on these moments, they appear longer because we have more detailed recollections to draw upon.

Conversely, during periods of boredom or sadness, time can feel as though it is dragging. In these states, fewer memories are created, and the lack of engaging stimuli can make the passage of time seem slower. This is because our brains are not as actively processing information, leading to a perception that time is moving more sluggishly.

Overall, emotions act as a lens through which we experience time, altering its flow based on the intensity and nature of our feelings. This subjective experience of time highlights the intricate connection between our emotional states and our cognitive processes.
